newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Donors return to African Devt Bank after reform.
newsitem.headline: Donors return to African Devt Bank after reform.

text.p: The annual meeting of the African Development Bank (AfDB) this week promises to be the least acrimonious in years after a management cleanout that has reconciled Western donors to the organisation.

The change in atmosphere is due in large part to the efforts of Omar Kabbaj, the Moroccan who took over as president in 1995 and restructured the bank, introducing strict lending and recruitment criteria in order to turn it around.
The three-day meeting starts on Wednesday.

"We have now reached the stage where I can say the Bank has become normal again, after a year and a half of intensive reforms," Kabbaj told Ivory Coast's Fraternite Matin newspaper last week. "The Bank has restored its credibility."

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, during a review of multilateral institutions, said in February: "The most far-reaching success story is the turnaround of the African Development Bank, which has tightened its lending rules, cut staff by 20 percent and appointed external auditors."
The AfDB's headquarters are in Ivory Coast's commercial capital, Abidjan, and its annual meeting will be held in the city from May 28-30.
The one issue that might trouble proceedings is the capital increase Kabbaj is seeking.

African nations, which hold two thirds of the shares, support him but are unwilling to cede more influence to Western countries which currently hold the rest of the shares and will probably have to find the bulk of the new capital.
Kabbaj said in the interview there was no pressing need for capital and that the Bank was aiming for an increase by 1999.
"For the Bank's operations, we can live without a capital increase for three or four years," he said.

"Having said that, we need this increase to consolidate our credibility on the international financial markets, to improve our ratios, to protect ourselves against difficult conditions in several countries in the future and also to allow us to develop the private sector more."
The private sector will be very much to the fore at the annual meeting and at a series of seminars in the days before.
Private investors are showing increasing interest in Africa -- happily, since Western nations are finding it harder and harder to convince taxpayers at home to provide more aid.

However, after withholding cash for two years until management reforms were brought in, Western states finally replenished the Bank's soft loan arm, the African Development Fund (ADF), in May and it began lending again last September.
Under the new regime, only 14 creditworthy African states are able to borrow from the Bank on commercial terms. The other 39 have to rely on the ADF, and the Western withdrawal hurt.
Its annual report shows that the Fund was lending over $1 billion a year in the early 1990s. That was down to $894 million in 1993, and in 1994 and 1995 there were no new loans.
Kabbaj said the group was now geared up to provide $2.5 billion in loans per year, around half in the form of interest-free lending from the ADF.
